# Chained Workflows {#sec-chained-workflows}

Generative AI models aren't just powerful in isolation - they become transformative when woven throughout your workflow.
Instead of using the model as a thought partner or a colleague to help with some task, you can link together tasks to automate _entire processes_, effectively creating your own team of AI agents.

Chaining also makes debugging and refinement easier. 
If an error appears in the final result, you can isolate which link in the chain failed or didn't work as expected (remember the `medial heel` example?), and then you can iterate on that step until it's working as expected. 
This modularity mirrors good measurement practice: test and validate each subcomponent of a process before interpreting the final results.
It's similar to having an error in your data cleaning that leads to an erroneous statistical conclusion.

Metaprompting is useful before you start chaining prompts together. If each step has its own prompt, each prompt should be reviewed, tested, and revised before its output becomes the input to the next step. Otherwise, a small ambiguity early in the chain can quietly shape everything downstream.

If you've heard of "multi-agent systems" before, you may be wondering if chained workflows are examples of these systems. The answer is _it depends_.
(Unsatisfying, I know.)
In general, the purpose of both processes is the same - breaking down a sophisticated process into discrete tasks - but the implementation of this process varies a bit when comparing chained workflows and multi-agentic systems.

Chained workflows can be thought of as explicit sequences of model calls with structured state passed from one step to the next. Each step may use the same model, different models, or tools; the important feature is that the workflow specifies how outputs become inputs for subsequent steps. Multi-agent systems extend this pattern when multiple role-specific agents interact or are coordinated by an orchestrator (e.g., one generates items, another reviews for fairness, and a third formats the output).

Although implementing multi-agent systems properly requires more engineering than most educational researchers need, understanding the connection is useful.
Chaining is the conceptual and methodological bridge to multi-agent workflows. 
The same logic (task decomposition, model-to-model communication, and iteration) underpins both. 
By designing your LLM tasks as transparent, stepwise processes now, you build a foundation that can later evolve into more automated and collaborative systems when institutional infrastructure or tooling catches up.

OpenAI announced [AgentKit](https://openai.com/index/introducing-agentkit/) in October 2025 as a set of tools for building, deploying, and evaluating agents. However, the current announcement says that Agent Builder and Evals are being wound down after November 30, 2026; it recommends the [Agents SDK](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/agents) for code-based workflows and [Workspace Agents in ChatGPT](https://openai.com/index/introducing-workspace-agents-in-chatgpt/) for natural-language-oriented workflows. Product names and availability in this area are moving quickly, so treat this paragraph as a dated example rather than a permanent recommendation.

I'm being a bit hand-wavy here because this is still new to me (AgentKit was introduced at the [OpenAI Dev Day](https://openai.com/devday/) on October 6, 2025), but I expect to dive into designing multi-agent systems in the next few months. Check back later if you're interested to see what I learn!

## Prompt Chaining vs. Multi-Agent Systems

I asked ChatGPT 5 to make a table describing the differences between the two. I'm not completely sold on some of the distinctions made below, but here is the table nonetheless. The comparison describes common patterns, not requirements; a framework can make a chained workflow more autonomous, or a multi-agent workflow more explicit and tightly controlled.

| Feature               | Prompt chaining                                                        | Multi-agent system                                               |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Primary pattern       | Sequential prompts where each step consumes the previous step’s output | Multiple specialized agents coordinated by an orchestrator       |
| Orchestration         | You (or your code) dictate the next step explicitly                    | Orchestrator/agents decide routing, handoffs, and tool calls     |
| Modularity            | Explicit steps are easy to inspect; reuse depends on implementation    | Roles can be reusable, but coordination adds complexity           |
| Autonomy              | Usually low; routing is specified by code or configuration             | Can be higher, but depends on the orchestrator and guardrails     |
| Parallelism/branching | Must be designed explicitly                                            | Often supported by the framework, but not automatic              |
| Tool integration      | Possible and usually wired into individual steps                        | Possible through agents, tools, or an orchestrator                 |
| State & memory        | Passed or stored explicitly by the workflow                             | May be managed across handoffs, depending on the framework        |
| Error handling        | Must be implemented at the relevant steps                               | May include retries or validation, but these still require design |
| Best for              | Simple, inspectable multi-step workflows                                | Complex workflows with distinct roles or dynamic routing          |
| Cost/complexity       | Lower to build/maintain for small tasks                                | Higher initial setup; scales better for complex use cases        |
